title: How the alpha.school '2-hour school' frightened me and then didn't
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton examines the pitch for alpha.school, a US network that says AI lets children master academics in two hours a day. After looking closely at the video and website he concludes that no two-hour school exists, because the claim rests on a narrow US usage of academics as knowledge in maths, reading, science and social studies. Through his own knowledge, skills and understanding framework, the morning block is AI-supported knowledge learning and the afternoon is skills learning with performance assessment, so the school really runs a six-hour learning day. He praises its efficient handling of knowledge, which frees time for slower skills and understanding, but criticises the marketing for devaluing the skills work and for siloing the two kinds of learning.
points: The two-hour school is a framing effect: academics means knowledge, and the afternoon skills work is learning too.
If the adaptive AI works, it delivers the repeated experiences that make knowledge sticky quickly, which is a real strength.
Efficient knowledge learning matters mainly because it frees scarce time for skills development and reflection, which take much longer.
The school's own story undersells the skills afternoon, and separate knowledge blocks risk siloing subjects.
quotes: I bring you news. There is no such thing (yet) as a 2-hour school. It’s a matter of culture and semantics.

Assuming the AI program and adaptive apps is good, what we have, therefore, is an individually learning-focused program for each child that delivers the repeated experiences that help the children make their knowledge learning sticky. The implication of the video is that their children’s learning gets to sticky faster than it does in other kinds of school.

To be honest, I was a little concerned about that sentence about parents not wanting children to go home after two hours. It implies that the rest of what is done during the day is in response to parents not wanting the inconvenience of their children coming home too early.

Third, as you might expect, I would define what is going on in the afternoon as learning in the same way that the morning is described as learning. Through my lens, the school has a two-hour morning learning block that is mainly focused on knowledge and another learning block focused on skills in the afternoon. This seems like learning to me.
Fourth, it feels like a missed opportunity that the alpha.school story mostly focuses only on knowledge learning. It devalues something that Mackenzie Price herself says ‘matters most’.

Sixth, in dealing with the academics in 25-minute separate blocks in the morning and skills learning in the afternoon, the approach risks putting different kinds of learning into silos. I have said before that whilst it is important for children and students to see different subjects as having their own knowledge, skills and conceptual frameworks, it is also important in the 21st century to see how they connect with each other, too.
Within the general context of US approaches to school, alpha.school is offering something different. But it is not offering a 2-hour learning school. A 2-hour learning school doesn’t exist.
